newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters says wants low NZ inflation all of the time.
newsitem.headline: Peters says wants low NZ inflation all of the time.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters said on Thursday relaxation of the Reserve Bank's inflation band was not a licence to go soft on inflation which he wants kept low all of the time.
"Any temporary relief would soon be eroded by rising costs," Peters told a government to business summit.

"In changing the inflation band, the government did not give the Reserve Bank governor licence to go soft on inflation. He has signed an agreement that he will work at all times to aim to keep inflation in a band of 0-3 percent.
"What we have done is give him some room to more smoothly manage monetary operations, but we still expect him to keep inflation low all of the time," Peters said.
The new National-NZ First coalition government, formed in December, widened the target band for underlying inflation to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
"After three years of rapid rises in the dollar its velocity has been arrested. In short, we didn't lose our nerve," he said.

"Business has been concerned that increased government spending announced in the coalition agreement, and further clarified in the BPS (Budget Policy Statement), will add to inflationary pressure, increasing the likelihood that the New Zealand dollar will continue to appreciate.

"We are not oblivious to these concerns. In light of increased spending, we have looked at the balance between government spending, tax reduction and debt repayment, and that is why we have postponed tax reductions scheduled for July 1, 1997 to July 1, 1998.
"In fact we will be running a bigger fiscal surplus for 1997/98 than last year's budget projected.
Peters said fiscal projections of the BPS had been criticised as highly optimistic.
"Well, don't fall prey to the scaremongering tactics of a few commentators who focus on two things -- the risk of fiscal creep and 'over-optimistic' Treasury forecasts.

"They may be right to urge caution, but they have no right to invoke alarmism, for this government is committed to prudent and safe fiscal management. We have gone further than previous governments by explicitly setting out the costs for all three budgets of this parliamentary term.
Peters recent GDP (gross domestic product) figures suggested doom and gloom merchants are wrong.
GDP was, on average, 2.7 percent higher in 1996 than in 1995, in line with Treasury expectations.
Even if there was no growth in the March quarter, annual average growth for 1996/97 will be around 2.5 percent, well above the expectations of the market, he said.
Debt repayment remained a priority even though it was being reduced at a slower rate than the previous government, he said.
"Our goal in the long term is to reduce gross Crown debt below 30 percent of GDP and net Crown debt to below 20 percent of GDP.
"This government intends to maintain fiscal surpluses so that we can make further progress on reducing debt and boosting national savings."
